title: Dark blood, chest pain, rising potassium
note: Fictional patient. DRAFT pending clinical sign-off. Doses and energies are quoted from the 2025 AHA guidelines (and the ERC where named) for recognition; your unit protocol, crash-cart stock and the attending nephrologist come first. Simulation success is an educational result, not a prediction of patient survival.
intro: At 8:30 a.m., Mrs. Linda Ocampo, 61, at Station 9 reports back and chest pain and nausea. The blood in her venous line looks translucent, like red wine. Two minutes later, the patient at Station 10 says his back hurts.

n1.prompt: What do you do at Station 9?

choices.text: Stop the pump, clamp the lines, do not return the blood; monitor; urgent potassium and hemoglobin; call the physician-on-duty.
choices.feedback: Hemolyzed blood carries potassium and is never returned.

choices.text: Return the blood and end the session.

n2.scene: Station 10 has the same symptoms; his venous line also looks abnormal.
n2.prompt: What does the charge nurse do?

choices.text: Declare a possible cluster: stop and clamp at Station 10, check every patient on the same water and concentrate, hold new starts, call the Medical Director; technician keeps lines and samples water and fluid.
choices.feedback: Hemolysis is often a shared supply fault.
A cluster needs immediate action across the unit.
choices.then: You declare the cluster five minutes later.

n3.scene: Mrs. Ocampo’s potassium is 7.4 mmol/L; the ECG shows peaked T waves. At 8:55 she becomes unresponsive and pulseless.

choices.text: Cardiac arrest: CPR, arrest algorithm, potassium treatment per protocol; blood still not returned; the watcher covers Station 10 and the rest.
choices.feedback: Potassium is the reversible cause; the circuit decision stays.
Station 10 is also affected and needs a watcher.
choices.then: The charge nurse sends one nurse back to Station 10.

end.title: 10:00 a.m.
end.text: Mrs. Ocampo has ROSC and is transferred; the patient at Station 10 is stable. The water team finds a carbon tank breakthrough. No treatment restarts until the water and fluid are cleared.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Port-wine blood is never returned.
  • One hemolysis can be a cluster: check everyone on the same supply.
  • Potassium drives the arrest risk; keep a watcher for the other patients.
